extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics) / readers studying Kant's Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for aesthetic judgement (taste) as presented in the Critique of Judgment: what makes a judgement of beauty valid, how it claims universality, and how it differs from cognitive or moral judgements. Useful for analyzing/philosophically evaluating aesthetic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty judged by purposiveness of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements of taste about the Beautiful in nature concern satisfaction or dissatisfaction in the form of the object — i.e. the object's purposiveness as shown in its figure, not by reference to other objects or concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate beauty by how the object's form manifests a purposiveness that harmonises with our cognitive faculties (imagination and understanding) in the act of apprehension; do not reduce beauty to relations to other objects or to conceptual predicates. Example: the flower's form, not its smell, grounds a claim to be called beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective purposiveness / free play of faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste rests on a feeling of subjective purposiveness: a harmonious, purposive relation between Imagination (in its freedom) and Understanding (in its conformity to law) in the representation of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an aesthetic judgement, look for evidence that the spectator experiences a 'free play' between imagination and understanding — a pleasurable mental state produced by their reciprocal activity — rather than any conceptual or utilitarian purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim to universal validity (subjective universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste, although subjective, claims the assent of every one — i.e. it asserts a universal validity a priori despite not being a cognitive judgement based on concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the judgement presents itself as something that should be universally communicable (a rule for all subjects). Note that this universality is not inferable from concepts but is asserted on the basis of the perceived communicability of the feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity without conceptual proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements of taste assert necessity (they demand assent) but this necessity does not depend on a priori conceptual proofs or logical grounds; it is a non-cognitive, a priori claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject attempts to ground aesthetic necessity in syllogistic proof or conceptual demonstration; instead examine whether the judgement appeals to an a priori feeling of necessary agreement rooted in the mental state of judging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of taste (judge oneself)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove taste, the subject must judge by himself (autonomy), without relying on the empirical judgements or applause of others; making others' judgements the ground of one's own would be heteronomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating claims of beauty, privilege first-person reflective judgement exercised independently of social pressure or appeals to authority. Anti-pattern: changing one's judgement merely to gain applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not determinable by rules or concepts (non-cognitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no objective principle of taste under which one can subsume an object and infer by syllogism that it is beautiful; taste is not a cognitive judgement subsumable under concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of prescriptive rule-sets or formulaic lists that claim to determine beauty universally; critics' rules may guide or correct taste but cannot serve as the determining grounds for an aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: No empirical ground of proof (neither consensus nor sensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the agreement of others (empirical consensus) nor the mere enumeration of agreeable sensory ingredients can force assent to a judgement of taste; the aesthetic judgement is not provable by such empirical grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing an aesthetic claim, do not treat popularity or sensory composition as decisive proof. Example anti-patterns: relying on critics' authority or the majority's praise as proof of beauty; arguing from ingredients (the dish example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensus communis / communicability of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste can be conceived as a sensus communis — a communal sense that abstracts from private conditions by taking into account, a priori, the possible mode of representation of all others; taste judges the universal communicability of feelings without reference to concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a judgement reflects an attempt to imagine others' responses (putting oneself in the place of any other) and to abstract from private subjective contingencies. Use the three maxims: think for oneself, put oneself in others' place, and think consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste grounded in common cognitive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of universal communicability rests on shared subjective conditions of judgement — namely the common faculties (imagination and understanding) that are requisite for possible cognition in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming universal validity for an aesthetic judgement, justify it by appeal to the shared structure of cognitive faculties (not to concepts); show how the representation accords with the general conditions of judgement common to humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among types of pleasure (beauty vs enjoyment vs moral vs sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in the Beautiful is a pleasure of mere reflection (not of enjoyment, not moral, nor merely rational contemplation). The Sublime and moral pleasures have different grounds and may presuppose other feelings or concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate the type of pleasure involved: do not conflate sensory enjoyment (taste of food), moral satisfaction, or rational contemplation with aesthetic pleasure in beauty. The Sublime may involve a different (moral or supersensible) element and can claim universal participation on different grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction of judgements of taste (justify a priori claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because judgements of taste claim a priori universal validity, a Deduction is required to show how such judgements are possible — i.e. how the subjective principle of taste can validly be presumed for all subjects by reference to the faculty of judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an account provides a transcendental explanation (a Deduction) linking the mental experience of pleasure to the general conditions of judgement, thereby justifying the claim to universal validity without invoking concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste benefits from examples and cultural models but remains autonomous
rubrics_metrics.description: Although taste claims autonomy, examples (classical authors, models) serve to sharpen and educate taste; following exemplary works helps one discover principles within oneself rather than producing mere imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pedagogical or critical contexts, use canonical examples to cultivate taste, but ensure these examples guide the subject toward autonomous judgement rather than replace it with imitation. Anti-pattern: treating tradition as definitive proof of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical interest in the beautiful linked to sociability
rubrics_metrics.description: While a pure aesthetic judgement must have no determining interest, empirical interests may attach to beauty indirectly (e.g. sociability): beauty empirically interests us in society because we desire to communicate feelings and to be refined members of a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering motives behind aesthetic preferences, recognise social and empirical interests (sociability) as contingent add-ons that can motivate cultivation or appreciation of beauty, but distinguish these from the pure a priori judgement of taste.
